opus-5.5.text:
I think for me the shift happened pretty naturally. When I started out, I was really drawn to the algorithm side of reinforcement learning — the papers, the new ideas, trying to squeeze out better scores on benchmarks. But the more I actually ran experiments, the more I noticed that what slowed me down usually wasn't a lack of ideas. It was the tooling. Environments were slow, code was messy, results were hard to reproduce, and you'd spend days just getting a baseline to run correctly.

So I started building things to fix my own pain points. That's how projects like Tianshou and later EnvPool came about. With EnvPool, for example, the observation was simple: a lot of RL training time is just spent stepping environments, and if you can make that dramatically faster, every researcher using it gets to iterate faster. That kind of leverage felt more meaningful to me than producing one more algorithm paper that gives a small improvement on Atari.

I also came to believe that in RL, and in AI more broadly, infrastructure is kind of underrated. People talk about algorithms and models, but a lot of real progress comes from someone making the system reliable and fast enough that you can try ten times more things. When you work on infra, you're multiplying everyone else's effort. And honestly, I just enjoy it — there's something very satisfying about engineering work where you can measure the result clearly: it's faster, it's correct, people use it.

Later, when I joined OpenAI and worked on things like the RL systems behind post-training, that conviction got even stronger. At that scale, the infrastructure basically determines what research is possible. So I wouldn't say my interest changed away from RL — it's more that I found where I could contribute the most, and that turned out to be making the whole machine work.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual shift toward infrastructure because tooling problems limited research, but does not identify infrastructure becoming more stable as a possible reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that my interest in RL infrastructure didn't really change so much as it kept getting pulled toward wherever the actual bottleneck was.

When I started, I was mostly frustrated as a user. I wanted to run an algorithm, and the existing code was either tangled, slow, or impossible to reproduce. So I wrote Tianshou largely out of self-interest. I wanted a clean, modular PyTorch library where I could swap out a policy or a buffer without rewriting everything. At that stage, "infrastructure" to me meant good software engineering around algorithms: clear abstractions, tests, readable code.

Then as I ran more experiments, I noticed something that surprised me. Most of my wall-clock time wasn't being spent on the neural network at all. It was the environment. Python simulators, the GIL, process overhead, all of that. That's what pushed me toward EnvPool. The question stopped being "how do I implement PPO nicely" and became "why is my GPU idle ninety percent of the time?" Once you frame it that way, you're really doing systems work, not algorithm work, and I found I enjoyed that a lot more than I expected.

And then the field itself moved. RL went from being this somewhat niche thing on Atari and MuJoCo to being central to how large language models get trained. Suddenly the environment is a model generating text, the reward is another model or a verifier, and the "simulator" is a distributed inference cluster. The core problems are the same, keeping the hardware busy, moving data efficiently, making things reproducible, but the scale and the stakes are completely different. So my interest shifted again, toward how you build training loops where generation and learning are decoupled, how you handle off-policy data responsibly, how you make the whole pipeline debuggable when a single run costs real money.

If I had to summarize it, I'd say I've always been drawn to the part of the problem that was quietly limiting everyone else. Early on that was code quality. Later it was environment throughput. Now it's the full systems picture around large-scale RL. I don't think I chose infrastructure as a topic. It's more that every time I tried to do the research, the infrastructure was in the way, and fixing it turned out to be the more interesting thing.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is less about losing interest in reinforcement learning and more about figuring out which parts of the work I enjoy. There’s the algorithmic side, and then there’s the infrastructure that makes it possible to run experiments, understand failures, and iterate quickly. I find that connection interesting: how the systems you build shape the research you can actually do.

At the same time, I don’t think of that interest as fixed. I’m still figuring out how close I want to be to the research questions versus building the tools that help people explore them. For me, it’s about finding where I can contribute and keep learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my interest has shifted from the algorithms themselves toward what makes experimentation possible. In reinforcement learning, an idea is only part of the work. You also need to collect experience, run experiments, and understand whether a result reflects a real improvement or just noise. Infrastructure shapes how quickly you can learn from that process.

So I see it less as moving away from research and more as becoming interested in the systems that support research. What appeals to me is shortening the distance between having a question and getting a trustworthy answer.

r001.rationale: The response says infrastructure supports faster, more reliable experimentation, but does not identify its gradual stabilization as a reason for the shift.
